heroText: Windhoek is Namibia's high-altitude capital, a tidy, German-influenced city ringed by the Khomas Hochland hills. First-time visitors should photograph the twin-spired Christuskirche, learn the country's history at the Independence Memorial Museum, and browse the stalls of Post Street Mall. Hosea Kutako International Airport sits east of the city, and Windhoek makes a natural staging point before heading into the Namib Desert or Etosha.

areas.name: City Centre
areas.text: City Centre holds Windhoek's main sights, banks and shops around Independence Avenue, easy to explore on foot in a day.

areas.name: Klein Windhoek
areas.text: Klein Windhoek is a leafy suburb east of downtown, home to guesthouses, restaurants and craft shops in a quieter setting.

areas.name: Ludwigsdorf
areas.text: Ludwigsdorf is an upmarket residential district with lodges and B&Bs, popular with travelers arranging Namibia-wide safari itineraries.

areas.name: Katutura
areas.text: Katutura is Windhoek's largest township, best visited with a local guide for its markets, murals and living history.

airports.name: Hosea Kutako International Airport (WDH)
airports.search: Hosea Kutako International Airport, Windhoek, Namibia
airports.text: Hosea Kutako International Airport lies about 45 kilometres east of the city; shuttle buses and pre-booked transfers are the easiest way into town.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Hosea Kutako International Airport (WDH) and central Windhoek before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Most first-time visitors base themselves in City Centre or Klein Windhoek for walkable access to the Christuskirche and Independence Memorial Museum, while Ludwigsdorf suits travelers organising onward safari trips. Windhoek works best as a one or two-night stop before heading further into Namibia.
hotelIntro: City Centre and Klein Windhoek hold most of Windhoek's guesthouses and mid-range hotels within easy reach of the main sights, while Ludwigsdorf's lodges suit travelers assembling gear or tours before a longer Namibia itinerary.
rentalCars: A rental car, often a 4x4, is standard for onward travel to Etosha, Sossusvlei or the Namib Desert, and most visitors collect one in Windhoek before departing the city.

travelTips.title: Use Windhoek as a staging point
travelTips.text: Plan one or two nights in Windhoek to collect a rental vehicle and supplies before heading into the Namib Desert or Etosha National Park.

travelTips.title: Visit Katutura with a guide
travelTips.text: Book a local guide for a Katutura township tour to see its markets and murals safely and with proper context.

travelTips.title: Layer for altitude
travelTips.text: Pack layers, since Windhoek sits over 1,600 metres above sea level and evenings can turn cool even in summer.

travelTips.title: Book safaris ahead
travelTips.text: Reserve onward safari lodges and park permits before arriving, since Etosha and other reserves can fill up in peak season.

The first known mention of the name Windhoek was in a letter from Jonker Afrikaner to Joseph Tindall, dated 12 August 1844. Early settlement In 1840 Jonker Afrikaner established an Orlam settlement at Windhoek.
Two Rhenish missionaries, Carl Hugo Hahn and Franz Heinrich Kleinschmidt, started working there in late 1842.
After a long absence, Hahn visited Windhoek again in 1873 and was dismayed to see that nothing remained of the town's former prosperity.
A request by merchants from Lüderitzbucht resulted in the declaration in 1884 of a German protectorate over what was called German South West Africa (Deutsch-Südwestafrika), now Namibia.
In June 1885, a Swiss botanist found only jackals and starving guinea fowl amongst neglected fruit trees.
Colonial Windhoek was founded on 18 October 1890, when von François fixed the foundation stone of the fort, which is now known as the Alte Feste (Old Fortress).
After 1907, development accelerated as indigenous people migrated from the countryside to the growing town to seek work.
In 1920, after the Treaty of Versailles, the territory was placed under a League of Nations Class C mandate and again administered by South Africa.

In 1971, the Namibian general contract workers strike started from Windhoek with the goal of abolishing the contract labour system, opposing apartheid, and promoting Namibia's independence. Since Namibian independence Since independence in 1990, Windhoek.
